summary: Describes problems with flow-based measurement, such as scalability, flexibility and export reliability, and shows how IPFIX Mediation may help. It gives examples of where mediation applies. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A middleman who collects, sums up and passes along traffic counts so many watchers each get what they need.

subtitle: How to handle flow measurement at scale using intermediary processors.

tldr.problem: Flow-based measurement systems face three challenges: coping with traffic growth exceeding collector capacity, supporting multiple applications with different measurement requirements, and dealing with heterogeneous equipment from different vendors.
tldr.mechanism: IPFIX Mediation introduces an intermediate device (IPFIX Mediator) positioned between exporters and collectors. This mediator transforms and aggregates flow records, adjusting granularity, correlating data, and filtering to match application and system needs.
tldr.outcome: Mediators enable scalable measurement systems that can serve diverse applications without overloading exporters or collectors. They can normalize data from legacy protocols, anonymize sensitive information, and adapt records to different network topologies.

facts.label: Architecture levels
facts.value: Original Exporter, Intermediate Process, IPFIX Mediator, Collecting Process

today: RFC 5982 is an informational guidance document describing the problem space and applicability of IPFIX Mediation. It remains current; IPFIX Mediation is deployed in production measurement systems at large service providers and enterprises.

sections.title: What is IPFIX Mediation
sections.content:
Flow-based measurement allows network operators to monitor large amounts of traffic at distributed observation points. However, when the same measurement infrastructure must serve multiple applications with different requirements, network equipment becomes overloaded. IPFIX Mediation solves this by introducing an IPFIX Mediator: a device positioned between exporters (routers and switches that create flow records) and collectors (analysis systems).

The IPFIX Mediator hosts one or more Intermediate Processes that transform the flow record stream. These processes can aggregate records, change granularity, correlate data across flows, apply filters, or convert between different flow export formats. The mediator can be a standalone box or functionality embedded in an exporter or collector.

This architecture fills a critical gap: exporters have limited CPU and memory for complex processing, and collectors should not be burdened with transformations that intermediate devices could perform. IPFIX Mediation lets administrators build scalable, flexible measurement systems by moving processing to the right place in the architecture.
sections.eli5: Routers send traffic counts to a middleman device instead of straight to the analysis computer. The middleman can combine counts, filter them, change their format, or send different versions to different places. This lets routers stay simple and analysis systems get exactly the data they want.

sections.title: Three Core Problems
sections.content:
IP traffic growth has overwhelmed single collectors. With 10 Gb/s links common and total traffic exceeding 100 Gb/s in enterprise networks, the volume of flow records from multiple exporters can exceed what one collector can handle. Reducing data at the exporter (through sampling, filtering, or aggregation) loses important information, making it hard to detect subtle traffic changes and anomalies.

Multiple application requirements demand different measurement setups. Some applications need flow-level detail; others want aggregates or packet-level information. Configuring an exporter to satisfy all requirements in parallel overloads its metering process. Instead, exporters should run simple measurement, and intermediate processing should adapt records for each application.

Heterogeneous environments use equipment from many vendors and software versions. Routers, switches, and probes have different metering capabilities and export formats. Some devices support only basic NetFlow exports; others support IPFIX. Collectors must understand all these formats and capabilities. A mediator between exporters and collectors can normalize and adapt records, hiding this complexity from collectors.

The solution requires a scalable, flexible collecting infrastructure with an intermediate mediation function. Early data reduction at exporters (sampling, filtering) must balance with keeping enough detail for accurate analysis.
sections.eli5: Too much traffic arrives to count it all at once. Different monitoring teams want different reports: billing wants sums by customer, security wants details, engineering wants path information. Old routers speak an outdated language, new ones use IPFIX. A mediator in the middle fixes all of this.

sections.title: How Mediation Works
sections.content:
Adjusting flow granularity is the simplest mediation function. Flows can be keyed on 5-tuple (protocol, source/destination IP, source/destination port), or on coarser keys like BGP autonomous system number or network prefix. A mediator can re-aggregate records with a new key set, reducing the number of records or grouping them differently for specific analysis tasks.

Spatial composition merges records from multiple observation points within or across networks. Link aggregation groups physical interfaces; records from multiple Exporters can be merged if they represent the same logical flow as seen from different points. A mediator correctly combines these records when measurement topology is known.

Time composition aggregates consecutive records with identical flow keys, creating longer time windows and enabling statistics like average, maximum, and minimum values computed from shorter intervals. This is equivalent to longer timeout settings on exporters but allows fine-grained monitoring of short-term changes.

Correlation enriches records by comparing them or combining them with external data. Examples: calculating one-way delay from packet timestamps at two observation points, computing rate-limiting ratios from ingress/egress records, or associating BGP attributes from routing table lookups.

Data filtering and distribution route records to different collectors based on content. A mediator can send IPv4 records to one collector, IPv6 to another, or distribute customer records by VPN identifier. This load-balances analysis systems and lets different teams analyze their data independently.
sections.eli5: A mediator groups flows differently (by customer instead of by port), combines counts from multiple routers for the same flow, extends time windows, adds extra information from routing tables, and sends different record types to different places.

sections.title: Real-World Use Cases
sections.content:
Data retention for legal compliance requires reliable export and massive storage. If UDP export loses records, a mediator can receive UDP from legacy exporters and forward over SCTP (reliable) to collectors, meeting regulatory requirements without upgrading all exporters.

Wide-area branch office export faces bandwidth limits. A mediator at the branch can aggregate and correlate records locally before sending a single compressed stream across the WAN, fitting multiple data types and volumes within constrained links.

Legacy protocol migration from NetFlow v9 to IPFIX lets old exporters continue sending NetFlow while a mediator converts to IPFIX format for modern collectors. This eases the transition during infrastructure upgrades.

Traffic engineering and capacity planning benefit from spatial composition. A mediator merges records from routers in different geographic areas to compute traffic matrices by source/destination prefix or AS number. This input feeds optimization algorithms.

Security and anomaly detection need detailed flow information. Rather than configuring exporters with heavy sampling, exporters send sampled data to a collector, then a mediator can re-combine multiple samples or apply selection thresholds (e.g., only export flows above 100 packets) to feed security analytics without overwhelming the system.
sections.eli5: Regulators require data for months: a mediator makes UDP reliable. Branch offices have slow links: a mediator compresses data before sending. Old routers only speak NetFlow: a mediator translates to IPFIX. Security needs flow details without overloading routers: a mediator filters and combines smartly.

sections.title: Implementation Challenges
sections.content:
Exporter information loss: When a mediator re-exports records, the Collector sees the mediator's IP address, not the Original Exporter's. The mediator must communicate the source exporter identity through additional Information Elements so collectors know which routers contributed the data.

Timestamp interpretation: IPFIX records include an Export Time (reference timestamp) and delta timestamps relative to that. If a mediator modifies the Export Time, delta fields become wrong. Mediators must preserve or recalculate these carefully.

Template ID management: Each Transport Session maintains its own Template ID space. If a mediator combines multiple incoming sessions into one outgoing session, it must remap Template IDs to avoid collisions and track which original (session, ID) pair maps to which output ID.

Options Template information: Some IPFIX records describe sampling rates and other metadata via Options Templates. If a mediator aggregates records with different sampling rates, it must report an adjusted sampling fraction to avoid collector miscalculation.

Network topology awareness: Aggregating records requires understanding whether summation makes sense. Merging records from multiple Exporters entering a domain is valid; merging packet counts from different observation points on the same flow may cause double-counting. The mediator must know the measurement topology.

Non-key field handling: IPFIX allows non-key fields like Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) to vary per packet. When aggregating flows with different DSCP values from different observation points, the mediator must decide: keep the first observed value, keep the last, report both, or remove the field.
sections.eli5: A mediator must remember which exporter sent which data, keep timestamps consistent, remap Template IDs correctly, report sampling rates after aggregation, understand the network layout, and decide what to do when aggregated records have conflicting values for the same field.
